title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals have deployed generative AI systems to enhance traditional fraud schemes in Georgia and South Florida by cloning voices from social media and creating deepfakes to impersonate trusted individuals like immigration attorneys. The failure is one of impersonation at scale: a technology built for synthesis was used to commit fraud without the victims having any reliable way to verify the identity of the person they were communicating with. No human verification step could have stopped this, since the victims believed they were interacting with someone they had independently chosen to trust.

The most prevalent form is the grandparent scam, where AI clones a relative's voice to request emergency money. A South Florida immigration attorney had his identity stolen to target immigrants seeking legal services. According to reported FBI data, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses in the year prior to these incidents, with Florida accounting for $39.9 million across 350 complaints and Georgia for $10.4 million across 71 complaints.

It is not established how the scammers obtained voice samples, whether any platform or service failed to prevent the creation or distribution of these deepfakes, or what technical measures might have prevented victims from being deceived.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit scams across Georgia and South Florida by creating deepfakes and cloned voices to impersonate trusted individuals. A South Florida immigration attorney discovered scammers had stolen his voice and identity to target immigrants, while a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. Florida experienced 350 AI-related complaints totaling $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints resulting in $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers use generative AI to make traditional frauds more convincing by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photographs, and researching victims' family connections. The grandparent scam, where criminals mimic a relative's voice to request emergency money, has become particularly prevalent. Financial institutions warn customers that AI makes impersonation increasingly difficult to detect. Experts recommend establishing family code words for verification, pausing before responding to urgent requests, and contacting banks directly rather than responding immediately to suspicious communications.
